source.title: Is interpolation benign for random forest regression?
source.authors: Ludovic Arnould; Claire Boyer; E. Scornet

record.tranche_reason: The study reports risk as sample size increases in interpolation-related regimes and argues that interpolation can coexist with consistency for random forests. This refines the claim’s scope but does not test model-size or epoch-wise double descent.
record.gate_note: The sample-size risk sweeps for KeRF, Median RF, and Breiman RF bear on V3. The paper also reports theoretical consistency bounds and interpolation-zone volumes, but these do not establish a fall-rise-fall test-risk curve or whether risk locally rises as sample size increases. Figure 2's plotted configuration labels do not clearly match the preceding prose, so those results are not separately extracted.
record.test_reason: The paper studies whether interpolating random forests are consistent, meaning excess risk goes to zero as n grows, with tree depth tied to n (about log2 n, or grown to pure leaves). Because capacity scales with n, every estimator interpolates at every n. No sweep crosses an interpolation threshold at fixed capacity, so no sample-wise peak (V3) can appear. There is no capacity sweep past the interpolation point (V1, V4), no epoch axis (V2), and no noise or regularization peak analysis (V6). The risk-vs-n curves measure a related construct, benign interpolation or consistency, not the double-descent shape. Double descent is only mentioned in the related-work framing (benign overfitting, Belkin et al., Buschjäger & Morik).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove that interpolation and consistency are incompatible for non-adaptive centered RF. KeRF is consistent, at a slow rate, in the mean interpolation regime. Interpolating Median RF is consistent, with the averaging from feature randomization as the key mechanism. Experiments suggest Breiman RF without bootstrap is consistent while exactly interpolating. Bootstrap also gives consistency but removes exact interpolation. The vanishing volume of the interpolation zone is a necessary condition. Interpolation is benign for consistency but can damage convergence rates.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines interpolation and consistency in random forests, using theoretical analysis and risk-versus-sample-size experiments rather than the original double-descent capacity/epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported regimes differ by forest type, depth/interpolation choice, and bootstrap or feature-randomization configuration. The paper argues that bootstrap affects whether the forest interpolates, while feature subsampling reduces but does not eliminate the interpolation area.

fits_no_version.finding: Interpolating forests have excess risk falling toward zero as n grows: KeRF in the mean interpolation regime, Median RF grown to pure leaves, and Breiman RF without bootstrap. Interpolation is benign for consistency but slows convergence rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolating (fully grown) random forests can be consistent: interpolation is benign in nonparametric ensembles.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory shows that interpolating non-adaptive centered RF are inconsistent because of empty cells (Prop. 3.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolation is malignant for non-adaptive random forests.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: Risk-versus-sample-size numerical results are shown in figures rather than tabulated with exact values. Experiments use finite forests and a limited set of regression models; the stated experimental repetitions are 30 for Figures 7, 8, and 11. The sample-size sweeps do not establish a general result about local risk increases near an interpolation threshold.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 Breiman RF results were not extracted separately because the conditions stated in the preceding prose do not clearly match the configuration labels in the figure. Figures 9 and 10 give additional model plots, but the relevant conditions and labels are not sufficiently clear in the provided text to assign separate results confidently.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; deep networks are not studied.
No fixed-capacity sample sweep near an interpolation threshold; capacity scales with n in every experiment.
No sweep of forest capacity (depth, number of trees) showing risk before and after the interpolation point.
No effective-complexity measure predicting a peak.
No analysis of a noise-driven peak, multiple peaks, or tuned regularization removing a peak.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 'challenges' label is withdrawn. A decreasing risk-vs-n curve for estimators whose depth grows with n tests consistency, not the near-threshold, fixed-capacity regime V3 describes. The Figure 2 legend ('mf=ceil(d/3)+1', 'bootstrap on, mf=d') indeed conflicts with the prose (bootstrap with mf=1 vs. no bootstrap with mf=ceil(d/3)). Figures 9, 10 and 14 also show legends inconsistent with their captions.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and peak near the training-set interpolation size.
Test error across training epochs or time.
The study tests sample-size trends in selected random-forest regimes, not whether a rise occurs for other model classes, settings, or a local range around the interpolation threshold.
Capacity sweeps across model classes and risk beyond the interpolation point.
A unified effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Whether noise or regularization drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimal regularization removes them.
Risk curves against an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: KeRF, Model 1
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated excess risk across increasing sample sizes in the mean interpolation regime.
rows.measure: empirical excess risk on the test set
rows.value: figure only; text says risk decreases toward zero as n increases
rows.uncertainty: mean ± std over 30 repetitions (displayed as a filled zone)
rows.note: The text reports the declining trend; the plotted numerical values are not stated.
rows.check: KeRF depth is set to floor(log2 n)+1, so capacity grows with n and the model is always past the interpolation threshold. A consistency curve cannot show V3's near-threshold rise. 'Reversed' is not warranted.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: KeRF in the mean interpolation regime, Median RF grown to pure leaves, and Breiman RF with max-features=1 and no bootstrap; tested regression models
reader_labels.reason: In the reported sample-size sweeps, excess risk declines rather than rises as n increases (rows r1–r12). This challenges a rise in these tested settings, without ruling out increases elsewhere.
